doc.title: Alicia Olatuja interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 9, 2018

title: Having an identity across genres: advice from an opera diva and Dr. Budds
summary: Asked about identity, she recounts asking an opera diva and professor Dr. Budds whether she must pick one genre.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: If you try to do everything do you risk not having an identity in the music business?

Nope. That’s a good question. That’s such a good question, and it’s something that I have had to answer and ask and question other people about since I was a freshman in college. And it’s been very interesting. I spoke with like this really amazing opera diva extraordinaire, and I said to her, you know, can I take classical technique and just learn how to work my instrument and then like sing in any genre I want? And she looked at me up and down. She was like, “I have no idea what you’re talking about.” Then she like flung her scarf and walked out the room all dramatic. And I was like, “Really?” And then I spoke with the music history professor, Dr. Budds, he’s actually quite brilliant. And I said to him, “You know, I love all different types of music and I feel like I’m being informed by all different types of genres. Do I have to pick one and shut the door on all these other ones. It makes me feel like I’m at a buffet and I’m just determined to eat the pasta.” And he said to me, he was like, “You know what? Just try to be good at one thing and then build on that.” But he said, “You can’t be bad at everything or mediocre at a bunch of things.” He said, “Really figure out what it requires to be excellent at something and then use that same method to be excellent at more and more things.” He was like, “And then you know whatever. People are way more forgiving and open to an artist who has already shown that they’re willing to be dedicated to an art form and really pour themselves into it and then transfer to other genres.”
